title: VirtualWorld: Graphs, Agents, Time, and Survival

outline.title: VirtualWorld: A Text Simulator Built Around a Property Graph
outline.angle: Open by dismantling the idea that VirtualWorld is merely a chatbot: the important state lives in a graph shared by the backend, frontend, rules, and save files.
points: VirtualWorld is a text-based simulation engine for AI beings, implemented as a Flask backend with a modular JavaScript browser client.
WorldGraph is the runtime source of truth: typed nodes are stored in an ID-keyed dictionary, while directed, typed relationships are stored in a list.
The graph supports adding, removing, querying, filtering, serializing, loading, and updating areas, ways, items, characters, triggers, and their relationships during play.

outline.title: Every Action Triggers tick_turn: Queue, Clock, and Decay
outline.angle: Follow one command from submission through actor selection, world effects, and time advancement; the action is only the visible part of a larger engine cycle.
points: VirtualWorld supports continuous, sequential, random, and d20 coordination modes; each player action triggers a full tick_turn cycle and advances game time.
The engine clock defaults to one minute per tick, while the referenced scenario configures five minutes per turn.

The turn queue reconciles living players into sequential, random, or d20+DEX order; completing a queue cycle increments the turn number, advances the world clock, and applies tick and decay effects exactly once.

outline.title: Why NPCs, LLM Agents, and Humans Share One Player Model
outline.angle: Place a deterministic NPC, an LLM agent, and a human behind the same controls to show that autonomy is a decision-loop choice, not a separate class of physics.
points: Soak NPCs, simple NPCs, LLM-driven agents, and humans all use the same Player model, actions, world state, and clock; only the decision controller and its cost differ.

Decision loops may be deterministic, scripted, or model-driven; LLM cognition can improve choices but cannot grant capabilities unavailable through the shared action system, and the engine must never act for a human.

The OpenAI-compatible LLM path supports multiple providers, endpoints, models, token and rate limits, streaming, and logging, while structured memory stores consolidate state for reasoning, reflection, editing, and tools.

outline.title: Character Position and Inventory Are Graph Edges
outline.angle: Forget conventional coordinates and container arrays: ask where an object is and the answer is a typed relationship in the same graph that stores the rest of the world.
points: A character's location is represented by one graph-edge anchor relative to room entities, using relations such as at, on, under, behind, and beside.
Physical actions automatically move the character to the relevant way or target and assign the corresponding spatial relation.
Items use 'in' edges for rooms and 'carrying' edges for players; taking an item moves that edge, and the legacy Player.inventory property is not used by engine operations.

outline.title: Temperature Is a Survival System, Not a Static Number
outline.angle: Turn an ambient weather value into a visible survival loop by following it through insulation, bodily drift, damage, death risk, narration, and the core-temperature bar.
points: Room temperature defaults to 21°C, while core body temperature starts at 37°C and drifts each tick as insulation, wind chill, and humidity alter the effective environmental pressure.
Extreme temperature can cause damage, limit HP regeneration, and kill a character through hypothermia or heat-stroke thresholds.
The core-temperature vital maps 25–45°C to 0–100%, adds a °C suffix, and changes from blue and green through yellow to red; narrative tiers use the effective feels-like temperature after insulation.

outline.title: Author a Runtime Graph, Then Reuse Entries Through Tags
outline.angle: Start with a blank scenario and show the two-stage authoring contract: first build an authoritative graph, then populate a reusable library without creating invalid furniture combinations.
points: Scenario JSON defines node schemas for areas, ways, items, characters, and triggers; characters and world lore live in authoritative top-level blocks, while the graph becomes the runtime source of truth.

The persistent library stores reusable entities under data/library/ with one JSON file per entry in type-specific directories for objects such as items, tags, areas, characters, conditions, triggers, behaviours, and structures.

Tags are case-insensitive classifiers, but the population chain applies stricter eligibility: an area's domain tags must match both the furniture role/domain tags and the item's domain tags, with roles determining valid placement targets.

outline.title: Inspector, Engine Config, and Event Export: Runtime Debugging
outline.angle: When runtime behavior looks wrong, move beyond editing JSON blindly: inspect the entity, tune the engine constant, and export the exact visible event stream.
points: The context-sensitive Inspector handles areas, items, ways, characters, memories, behaviours, and lore through a singleton architecture with centralized lit-html rendering, with panel.js owning panel writes.

Engine Config exposes values such as sound penetration, heat propagation, and light spill through /api/settings/engine_config; defaults can be overridden in data/engine_config.json without editing Python or restarting the server.

WorldExport.exportEventLog() writes the visible event stream to Markdown, distinguishes global event-sequence ticks from in-game world turns, and excludes filtered hidden logs such as disabled LLM logs.

outline.title: Library 2.0 Saves: Full Schema, Backups, and DiffModal Conflicts
outline.angle: End on the scary part of world editing: synchronization can destroy good data, so the workflow needs full-schema saves, backups, guarded writes, and explicit conflict choices.
points: Library 2.0 standardizes entity types around full-schema editors and safer save paths with backups and guarded writes to prevent silent losses from incomplete or unread writes.

DiffModal supports per-entry conflict resolution for memories, items, relationships, conditions, vitals, decay rates, and equipped slots, showing change counts, status badges, value comparisons, and select-all controls while retaining whole-category clobbering.

Scenario workflows distinguish autosaves, manual saves, and source scenarios; live autosave edits are never written back into source JSON, so restarting cannot be treated as saving over the authored scenario.

brief:
- **Platform architecture:** The Flask-and-JavaScript VirtualWorld is organized into documented subsystems with explicit code boundaries, invariants, configuration, and development history.
- **Unified actors and autonomy:** Humans, NPCs, and LLM agents share a `Player` model, world state, and action system while using deterministic, scripted, or model-driven decision loops with different costs and capabilities.
- **LLM and memory services:** An OpenAI-compatible client supports multiple providers, endpoints, models, token and rate limits, streaming, logging, and reactive behavior; structured memory stores consolidate state for reasoning, reflection, editing, and tools.
- **Temporal engine:** Configurable continuous, sequential, random, and d20 modes coordinate action-triggered ticks, initiative, queue cycles, world updates, once-per-turn effects, and clock advancement.
- **World graph and spatial model:** A typed property graph stores entities and directed relationships, while hierarchical scopes, standardized IDs, room and door nodes, movement, and contextual placement support loading, projection, and eviction.
- **World realism:** Categorized indoor and outdoor spaces connect through visibility, light and sound propagation, weather, needs, and emotional responses to make geography interactive and believable.
- **Inventory, items, and equipment:** Graph-backed items support containers, carrying, toggleable and consumable states, depletion, layered paperdoll slots, and weapon handling.
- **Environmental survival:** Vitals, insulation, wind chill, humidity, resistance, core-temperature drift, damage, regeneration limits, and extreme-temperature death model environmental pressure; the UI visualizes core temperature through a color-coded vital bar.
- **Gameplay rules engine:** Combat, conditions, durable traits, reusable and directed triggers, periodic effects, comparisons and bounded adjustments, and event recording provide reactive mechanics.
- **Library taxonomy and eligibility:** File-based reusable entities use case-insensitive tags, domain chains, and role rules to control filtering, mechanic availability, and valid furniture or scenario targets.
- **Library synchronization and safe editing:** Full-schema editors, world-library `DiffModal` synchronization, per-entry conflict resolution, backups, and guarded writes reduce duplication and data loss.
- **Scenario lifecycle:** Authoring schemas, scenario catalogs, reusable libraries, validation demonstrations, reviews, autosaves, manual saves, restarts, and GUI or API workflows support design through playtesting.
- **Narration modes:** Disabled, player-authored modal, and AI-generated room and action descriptions stay synchronized across backend settings and frontend presentation.
- **Interface and observability:** Deferred lit-html bootstrapping, modular views, centralized Inspector rendering, map and observer views, filter-aware reports, Markdown event-log export, settings routes, and IndexedDB configuration expose and manage runtime state.
- **Project evolution:** Release histories, patch notes, repository work, test cleanup, completed systems, and remaining priorities such as biome-weighted resource generation document maturity and roadmap direction.
